rules.statement: Do not use Entity Framework Core set-based operations such as `ExecuteDeleteAsync` or `ExecuteUpdateAsync` in stores; load the rows and remove or update them through the change tracker so the change is saved with the unit of work.
rules.why: Not every provider supports set-based operations. The EF InMemory provider used by the hermetic host does not, so every prune failed. A set-based delete also runs outside the unit of work.
rules.check: Look for `ExecuteDeleteAsync`/`ExecuteUpdateAsync` calls, or provider-specific branches that fall back to them, in store or repository code.

rules.statement: Delete or prune large or unbounded sets of rows in bounded batches, each in its own unit of work, and repeat while the last batch came back full; never load the whole set into one unit of work.
rules.why: A single unbounded unit of work loads everything at once, for example a whole day of every tenant. Bounded batches keep memory use small and let a long backlog drain in many small units of work.
rules.check: Look for removal or cleanup code that queries all matching rows with no limit/Take, or that saves everything in one SaveChanges, and for removal store methods that take no batch limit.

rules.statement: When a batched delete's save fails with a concurrency exception because another replica deleted the same rows, treat it as progress and go on to the next batch instead of treating it as a failure.
rules.why: Losing the race means another replica already removed rows from that batch, so the work is getting done. Concurrent pruners waste at most one batch.
rules.check: In multi-replica cleanup loops, check that a store concurrency exception on save is caught and the loop goes on reading the next batch, rather than aborting or logging an error.

rules.statement: When a periodic maintenance task fails, log the failure and leave the work unmarked as done so it runs again at the next scheduled run; do not mark it complete or put off the retry for a long time.
rules.why: Marking it done or waiting a day after a failure hides a real failure and can mean the work never gets done.
rules.check: Look at background or hosted service catch blocks: the 'last completed' marker should only be set on success, and the failure should be logged.
